segments.title: Chương 268: 0270【Sự kiện lan rộng】
segments.content:
Not only did Zhang Chaoyang have Sohu News go full throttle, but he also personally got in on the action by writing a blog post.

It was the perfect opportunity to give his Sohu blog some extra exposure.

The title of Zhang Chaoyang's blog post was: "On the Basic Qualities of an Internet Giant's CEO."

He didn't name names, but everyone knew who he was mocking:

"...As the CEO of an internet giant, yet unaware that China and the United States are the world's largest internet markets..."

"As a publicly listed Chinese internet giant, yet surrendering without a fight before Japanese counterparts... and even willingly taking a backseat to Vietnam..."

"Speaking at the main forum of the China Internet Conference, yet riddled with errors and inexplicably belittling peers. Has someone put a curse on him? Or is he just sleep-deprived and not fully awake?"

"I think a certain someone should enroll in an MBA program for some further study. But perhaps, New Oriental is a better fit for him."

Within a day, this blog post surpassed 100,000 views.

Many netizens who weren't Sohu Blog users heard the news and flocked over just to watch the drama unfold.

It actually brought a lot of traffic to Sohu Blog and even boosted its registered user count.

The netizens were having a blast feasting on the gossip.

The last sentence of the article even became a popular catchphrase, evolving online into "New Oriental is a better fit for you."

New Oriental's chairman, Yu Minhong, was a rather sentimental person. He was still sticking with BlogCN (Bokee).

Finding his blog comments suddenly exploding for no apparent reason, Yu Minhong did some research to figure out what was going on. He then wrote a blog post specifically to mediate the dispute.

His entire article could be summarized in one sentence: "There's no need to argue like this. We're all bosses of listed companies. If this drags on, it won't reflect well on any of us."

Guess what the keyword was?

Listed companies!

New Oriental had just gone public this month.

Was Yu Minhong really here to mediate? He was here to show off that his company was now listed, that he was a boss of a listed company just like Li Yanhong and Zhang Chaoyang.

Chen Guiliang's statements, on the other hand, birthed even more golden phrases.

"Only old people can't sleep."

"Your subjects are ready to fight to the death, why does Your Majesty wish to surrender first?"

"I've only ever seen people fight for food, never for shit."

"Some people aren't stupid, they're just playing dumb."

On Chen Guiliang's Xiaonei and Hainei personal pages, many netizens left comments, hoping he would write an article about the matter.

Chen Guiliang obliged and wrote a piece titled: "I Won't Bother Others Unless They Bother Me. But If They Bother Me, Then F*ck It!"

He claimed that he wasn't intentionally picking a fight, but was forced to retaliate.

"As everyone knows, this was my first time speaking at such a major event. I was nervous, as if treading on thin ice. While it didn't keep me up at night, I did spend several days wracking my brain to revise the speech..."

"And what was the result? The theme of my speech was the future of web2.0, but before I even took the stage, someone was already saying web2.0 had no future..."

"What else could I do? Pretend I didn't hear it, play deaf and dumb, and just mindlessly read my script?"

However, the netizens' focus on his article was on the word "."

Everyone started asking what dialect "tā mā de" was from.

And since this character was difficult to type, netizens looked it up in the dictionary and unanimously switched to the character "怼" (duì). Besides the different tone, "怼" was more visually expressive and easier to understand.

On platforms like Tieba and various forums, netizens would say "怼他妈的" (duì tā mā de - f*cking attack him) at the drop of a hat.

Or they'd say, I'll f*cking school you!

The Southern Metropolis Daily had previously reported that the battle between Baidu and Sohu was a farce, and this time, it quickly published a commentary.

An excerpt is as follows:

"For some unknown reason, Baidu, which was criticized by Sohu just two months ago for its blind expansion into web2.0, had Li Yanhong publicly express concerns two months later that web2.0 would trigger an internet bubble. This, in turn, provoked Chen Guiliang of Bytedance..."

"Even more神奇 is that Zhang Chaoyang, who had repeatedly badmouthed web2.0, this time stood with Chen Guiliang, staunchly supporting the web2.0 development model..."

This report from the Southern Metropolis Daily was laugh-out-loud funny.

The reversal in Li Yanhong's and Zhang Chaoyang's statements made it seem like the two had swapped brains.

A couple of lunatics!

The truly sharp-tongued one, however, was Computer World.

This publication would later release an industry-shaking report titled "The Damn Tencent," furiously condemning Tencent for getting into every line of business and driving countless competitors to their deaths.

This time, Computer World's headline was: "A Dog-Eat-Dog Squabble."

In the article, the author mocked Li Yanhong for being blinded by money, having lost his basic human conscience. From the lightning-fast layoffs to reneging on stock options, he had already crossed the bottom line for an entrepreneur. He was madly pushing into web2.0 himself, yet he came out to badmouth the entire industry. Either he didn't bring his brain, or he didn't bring his conscience.

Then it mocked Zhang Chaoyang, saying he'd drunk himself silly with female celebrities. He was running Sohu Blog on one hand, while claiming web2.0 was a bubble on the other. Just after blasting Baidu for its blind foray into web2.0, he turned around and joined forces with Chen Guiliang, a web2.0 supporter. Despite having a head start, Sohu's search and blog businesses were always trailing behind, sniffing others' farts.

It then teased Chen Guiliang for being a clever little devil, taking advantage of Li Yanhong's nonsensical speech to launch a relentless attack and establish his own position as an industry leader. In reality, Chen Guiliang knew full well that Li Yanhong's and Zhang Chaoyang's concerns were valid, but he deliberately inflated the bubble for his own company's sake.

After reading the article, Chen Guiliang, while cursing inwardly, couldn't help but admire it: What a sharp judge of character!

Damn it, this crappy publication was invested in by IDG.

Is it really appropriate for you to bash one of your own like this?

In fact, wasn't Baidu also one of their own? IDG had started divesting from Baidu in February of this year, and still had a tiny bit of stock left to sell.

The Beijing News, which had previously deliberately contradicted and condemned Chen Guiliang because of the San Guo Sha report on Xinwen Lianbo, once again turned its guns around and strongly supported Chen Guiliang this time.

The Beijing News's stance remained unchanged: go with whatever sells.

Because Baidu was a behemoth and Chen Guiliang was a small fry, supporting Chen Guiliang brought infinite benefits. The Beijing News could both win public favor and seize the opportunity to sell papers with a hot topic.

The Beijing News's headline was: "Bytedance Challenges Baidu: A Suicidal Charge."

It portrayed Chen Guiliang as a righteous idealist, launching a fearless and tragic challenge against an industry giant.

The China Computerworld, an authoritative IT media outlet under the Ministry of Information Industry and hailed as the bellwether of China's IT industry, ran with this headline: "Internet Professionals Should Strengthen Their Own Professionalism."

The entire article didn't name anyone, but everyone knew it was criticizing Li Yanhong.

Clearly, Li Yanhong's unsubstantiated claims during his speech, saying China's internet penetration rate was lower than Vietnam's and that the market value of Chinese internet companies was less than a tenth of Japan's, had greatly displeased the supervising leaders.

If no one had exposed it, it would have been one thing; the leaders probably didn't know the real situation.

But with Chen Guiliang exposing it on the spot, what would the leaders be thinking?

This incident even spread to Hong Kong, and then to Singapore.

Singapore's Lianhe Zaobao, which particularly enjoyed following news from China, published a full-page article providing comprehensive coverage, including a detailed introduction to Chen Guiliang's background and resume.

Now, even the ordinary people of Singapore knew about a very young new tycoon in China's internet industry.

But the reports from the Hong Kong media were the most entertaining. Each headline was incredibly sensational:

"Computer Whiz Kid Crashes Internet Conference: Chen Guiliang Hands Out 'Red Packets' in Public, Li Yanhong Leaves with a Dark Face!"

"Baidu Boss in Hot Water! Speech Fumbles, Gets Trampled by Newbie, Big Shot Loses Face and Walks."

"Internet Wulin Conference Takes a Turn: Newcomer Knew Baidu Chief's Achilles' Heel and Exposed It on the Spot, Search Myth Shattered!"
